newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - February 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - February 5.

text.p: Following are the highlights of stories reported in the Irish press on Wednesday.
- The Irish government is actively considering a tribunal of inquiry to bring into the public domain further information about the Dunnes Stores payments to politicians controversy.
- Dublin city council's decision to issue 200 new taxi licences has been described by the Irish Taxi Federation as "ignorant" and a disaster for the trade.
- More than one child was abducted from Ireland every week last year.
- The Irish Prime Minister John Bruton demanded an apology from Britain for those killed in Bloody Sunday in Londonderry, Northern Ireland, but stopped short of calling for a new inquiry.
- The man most likely to be president of the new European Central Bank, Wim Duisenberg, has backed Ireland's case for membership of the first group moving to monetary union.

- Rank-and-file police in Ireland on Tuesday told the government to establish an independent commission to investigate their pay and conditions within three months or face consequences which "would be too horrible to contemplate".
- Irish Life on Tuesday night appealed to the remainder of its staff to agree to the recommendations of the Labour Court as a further 120 employees were suspended for rejecting new work practices.
- Two Filipino sailors were jailed for eight years on Tuesday for their part in a record cocaine seizure by customs investigators last summer.
- The Irish Farmers Association has threatened to make cattle prices an election issue unless the government takes positive action to tackle the crisis in the beef industry.
- A civil jury found O.J. Simpson liable for the stabbing deaths of his ex-wife and her friend, a moral victory for grieving relatives who felt the footballer got away with murder.
- A man was charged on Tuesday with murdering crime journalist Veronica Guerin.
- The state has demanded nearly 1.5 million Irish pounds be shaved off the legal bill facing taxpayers for two firms of solicitors which represented the Goodman group at the Beef Tribunal.

- Sharp selling of Irish government bonds by foreign investos on Tuesday reflects nervousness about the prospects for Irish membership of the single European currency and the state of the economy, analysts said.
